Happy New Year R-users!

Marissa Baskett and I would like to announce the following ECL298 for the upcoming quarter, Winter 2013:

Course title: Computational methods in population biology
ECL 298, CRN: 50354 (3 units, graded as S/U)

Course Description:
Numerical methods for simulating population dynamics using the computational software package R. An emphasis will be placed on model formulation and development, theoretical concepts and philosophical principles to guide simulation efforts, and implementing simulations with R. Topics covered may include simulation of difference/differential equations, matrix & continuously structured models, stochastic difference equations, and discrete/continuous-time Markov processes. Applications covered include structured population dynamics, spread of diseases, spatial spread of invasive species, population viability analysis, time series analysis of species interactions, and metapopulation and metacommunity dynamics.

Pre-requisites: a course in theoretical ecology (e.g., PBG 231 or an equivalent to ESP 121 from your undergraduate institution) or consent of instructor; no programming experience required.

Time: Mondays at 12:10-2:00pm plus an optional (but highly recommend) lab of structured work time on Fridays at 12:10-2:00pm, both in Wickson 2124. Note: The online scheduler incorrectly is reporting Tuesday as a meeting time.

Instructors: Marissa Baskett and Sebastian Schreiber

Attached is a syllabus for the course.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Has anyone tried to plot the terms from a GAM model with the partial residuals on the plot? The plot.gam function from the mgcv package does it quite well, but only for the non-parametric terms. It then passes any parametric terms of the model to the "termplot" function which refuses to put the residuals from a gam model on the plot.

I also tried putting just the parametric terms into the termplot function by itself, but when I asked it to give me the residuals it said:

Error in match.arg(type) :
  'arg' should be one of “deviance”, “pearson”, “scaled.pearson”, “working”, “response”

I have attached my data and code, if anyone can assist I would be eternally grateful.

--
Rosemary Hartman
UC Davis Graduate Group in Ecology
Dr. Sharon Lawler's Lab

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rosie,

The trouble seems to be that mgcv does not have a method for calculating partial residuals. That is, residuals.gam() won't take the argument type="partial". residuals.glm DOES have this method, though, and from my quick scan of the functions it should give you correct values. So, before running termplot, do this:
tmp.resid.gam <- residuals.gam

residuals.gam <- residuals.glm

Who knows what other functions this might break, so after you plot be sure to restore it with
residuals.gam <- tmp.resid.gam

Be sure to sanity check the values on your plot.

Noam

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The material I presented at this week's DRUG session can be found here:

http://www.noamross.net/blog/2013/1/7/collaborating-with-r.html

Also, we're looking for people to present in future weeks of our Wednesday work sessions.  These are informal, ~20 minute talks.  Let me know if you are interested.

Talks can be any of these formats:

 - "How to" - A quick introduction to a topic and pointers to more resources.  (Maybe something you just learned!)
 - "Show and Tell" - A cool thing you did in R
 - "Here's my problem" - take the group through what you're working on and solicit feedback

Here are some potential topics that people might want to discuss. Feel free to come up with others:

 - Best code organization practices (style guides)
 - Efficiency in coding - how to speed up your code
 - Options for coding interfaces (notepad++, RStudio...)
 - Version control (git)
 - Spatial analytics in R
 - Tools for genetics/bioinformatics in R
 - Producing reports with knitr/sweave
 - Modeling admixture hybridization packages.
 - MCMC and the STAN package
 - Monte Carlo simulations in R
 - Interfacing with other languages (why and when?)
 - Working with LOTS of data more efficiently
 - Cluster computing and parallel processing

I'm looking forward to a lot of interesting talks!

Noam

If you want a record of all your output for later access, dput() and dget() can be useful for storing/reading your list in a text file  as you iterate with your for loop. Once the simulation is complete, you can iteratively read in all the output into a single list (for loop again) for further analysis. Also, it might be worth looking into the foreach package and the %dopar% function, or the snowfall package. These packages allow you to utilize each core on your computer during simulation (called embarrassingly parallel processing). So, if you're using a quad-core machine, you can run your simulation in ~25-35% of the time it takes on a single core. R runs on a single core unless told to do otherwise.

I'm sure there's a better way to do this, these are just techniques I've figured out.

--Mason

messages.body_plain:
Arrays (multidimensional generalizations of matrices, sometimes called "tensors") are often faster than lists, and both options should be faster than dput.

Here's my R code trying out a simple example with 3-dimensional arrays.

I tried to include lots of comments, but it might not be clear in some places, so let me know if anything is confusing.

Dave

# pick the dimensions of the output array
l = 15  # rows of a single output matrix
m = 74  # columns of a single output matrix
n = 1000 # number of output matrices

# initializing the array ahead of time makes a big speed difference in R
A = array(dim = c(l, m, n))

# A function that returns a matrix of dimension l x m
f = function(l, m){
  tcrossprod(1:l, 1:m)
}

# For loops ---------------------------------------------------------------

# My understanding is that R works fastest if it fills in the last dimension
# of the array each time it goes through the for loop (the third dimension in
# this case).  Other orderings would work, but I think they'd be slower.
for(i in 1:n){
  A[, , i] = f(l, m) * i
}

# Then you can pull out matrices like you'd expect using R's subset notation

A[ , , 17] # the 17th l x m matrix

# a plyr way of doing things --------------------------------------------
library(plyr)
A2 = aaply(
  1:n,
  .margins = 1,
  .fun = function(i){f(l, m) * i}
)

# Note that plyr arranges the data differently from my for loop:
dim(A)
dim(A2)

# Otherwise, they return the same things:
all(A[ , , 10] == A2[10, , ])

# Timing ------------------------------------------------------------------

# we can compare how long the two methods take:
system.time(
  replicate(
    100, {
      A = array(dim = c(l, m, n))
      for(i in 1:n){
        A[, , i] = f(l, m) * i
      }
    }
  )
)

system.time(
  replicate(
    100, {
      aaply(
        1:n,
        .margins = 1,
        .fun = function(i){f(l, m) * i}
      )
    }
  )
)

# it looks like for-loops are *substantially* faster than plyr in this case.
# This may be because I'm using plyr improperly or in a way it wasn't intended

# For reference, let's see how much the whole array thing is slowing us down,
# by just running the function for making matrices without the array overhead.

system.time(
  replicate(
    100, {
      for(i in 1:n){
        sub.A = f(l, m) * i
      }
    }
  )

messages.body_plain:
A few hopefully useful thoughts: for loops are much maligned, but for applications like matrix projection models, where each step depends on the output of the last for are exactly the right tool for the job. If you are running the projection many times, it may be helpful to do some simple parallelization using plyr (which you can learn about today at the work session) to speed up the steps.

Once you have your matrices from the simulation, using vectorized tools like colMeans and the plyr or apply family of functions on the matrices will be the fastest way to summarize/manipulate the data. You may want to convert them to data frames using melt from the reshape2 package in order to do plotting.

As for storage, the most compact and fast way to save your simulation outputs would be to save the multidimensional matrices using save (for many R objects) or save.rds (for one R object), which create binary files. For longer term data storage, I would convert to a data frame and save as a CSV using write.csv.

I know this is the R user group list, but if you're doing the type of models Noam describes (each step depends on the last), you've profiled your code and there's nothing simple you can do to make it faster (and time is a limiting factor), you may wish to use Python with numpy <http://www.numpy.org/> or if you're up for a challenge interface C with R via .Call() (see the R Extension Manual <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html>).

If the problem is simply complexity of data structures, I agree with Dave 100% in that you should use multidimensional array approach. Also, if you guys are all doing similar population matrix models, and there is no existing library out for this (is there?), why not collaborate on a package and throw it on Github (and maybe CRAN too)? Your core code should be separate from your particular project's data anyways, and it's a lot safer.

Ross Ihaka and Duncan have a great presentation on implementing a 2D random walk without a for loop here: http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~ihaka/downloads/Taupo-handouts.pdf. Everyone's problem won't reduce to such a form, but if it does, being aware of such designs can save you a lot of frustration (and time).

just my two cents,
Vince

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions folks, I look forward to working with them.

I've been using a combination of the popbio library cran.r-project.org/web/ <http://cran.r-project.org/web/>packages/popbio/popbio.pdf and my own functions. popbio is pretty straightforward if you have copies of Caswell and Morris and Doak on hand.

On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 10:21 AM, Vince S. Buffalo <vsbu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I know this is the R user group list, but if you're doing the type of models Noam describes (each step depends on the last), you've profiled your code and there's nothing simple you can do to make it faster (and time is a limiting factor), you may wish to use Python with numpy <http://www.numpy.org/> or if you're up for a challenge interface C with R via .Call() (see the R Extension Manual <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html>).
>
> If the problem is simply complexity of data structures, I agree with Dave 100% in that you should use multidimensional array approach. Also, if you guys are all doing similar population matrix models, and there is no existing library out for this (is there?), why not collaborate on a package and throw it on Github (and maybe CRAN too)? Your core code should be separate from your particular project's data anyways, and it's a lot safer.
>
> Ross Ihaka and Duncan have a great presentation on implementing a 2D random walk without a for loop here: http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~ihaka/downloads/Taupo-handouts.pdf. Everyone's problem won't reduce to such a form, but if it does, being aware of such designs can save you a lot of frustration (and time).
>
> just my two cents,
> Vince

> On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 6:44 AM, Noam Ross <noam...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > A few hopefully useful thoughts:
> >
> > `for` loops are much maligned, but for applications like matrix projection models, where *each step depends on the output of the last* `for` are exactly the right tool for the job. > >

> > > Dave
> > >
> > > # pick the dimensions of the output array

> > >

> > > # of the array each time it goes through the for loop (the third dimension in

> > > }

> > >

> > >
> > >

> > > library(plyr)
> > > A2 = aaply(
> > >   1:n,
> > >   .margins = 1,

> > > )
> > >

> > > dim(A2)

> > > # Otherwise, they return the same things:

> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > # Timing ------------------------------------------------------------------
> > >
> > > # we can compare how long the two methods take:
> > > system.time(
> > >   replicate(
> > >     100, {

> > >       }
> > >     }
> > >   )
> > > )
> > >
> > > system.time(
> > >   replicate(
> > >     100, {

> > >         1:n,

> > >       }
> > >     }
> > >   )
> > > )
> > >

> > > # which isn't so bad.

> > On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 10:21 AM, Vince S. Buffalo <vsbu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I know this is the R user group list, but if you're doing the type of models Noam describes (each step depends on the last), you've profiled your code and there's nothing simple you can do to make it faster (and time is a limiting factor), you may wish to use Python with numpy <http://www.numpy.org/> or if you're up for a challenge interface C with R via .Call() (see the R Extension Manual <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html>).
> > >
> > > If the problem is simply complexity of data structures, I agree with Dave 100% in that you should use multidimensional array approach. Also, if you guys are all doing similar population matrix models, and there is no existing library out for this (is there?), why not collaborate on a package and throw it on Github (and maybe CRAN too)? Your core code should be separate from your particular project's data anyways, and it's a lot safer.
> > >
> > > Ross Ihaka and Duncan have a great presentation on implementing a 2D random walk without a for loop here: http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~ihaka/downloads/Taupo-handouts.pdf <http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/%7Eihaka/downloads/Taupo-handouts.pdf>. Everyone's problem won't reduce to such a form, but if it does, being aware of such designs can save you a lot of frustration (and time).
> > >
> > > just my two cents,
> > > Vince
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 6:44 AM, Noam Ross <noam...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > A few hopefully useful thoughts:
> > > >
> > > > `for` loops are much maligned, but for applications like matrix projection models, where *each step depends on the output of the last* `for` are exactly the right tool for the job.  If you are running the projection many times, it may be helpful to do some simple parallelization using `plyr` (which you can learn about today at the work session) to speed up the steps.
> > > >
> > > > Once you have your matrices from the simulation, using vectorized tools like `colMeans` and the `plyr` or `apply` family of functions on the matrices will be the fastest way to summarize/manipulate the data.  You may want to convert them to data frames using `melt` from the `reshape2` package in order to do plotting.
> > > >
> > > > As for storage, the most compact and fast way to save your simulation outputs would be to save the multidimensional matrices using `save` (for many R objects) or `save.rds` (for one R object), which create binary files.  For longer term data storage, I would convert to a data frame and save as a CSV using `write.csv`.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Jan 15, 2013 at 5:27 PM, Dave Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Arrays (multidimensional generalizations of matrices, sometimes called "tensors") are often faster than lists, and both options should be faster than dput.
> > > > >
> > > > > Here's my R code trying out a simple example with 3-dimensional arrays.
> > > > >
> > > > > I tried to include lots of comments, but it might not be clear in some places, so let me know if anything is confusing.
> > > > >
> > > > > Dave
> > > > >
> > > > > # pick the dimensions of the output array
> > > > > l = 15  # rows of a single output matrix
> > > > > m = 74  # columns of a single output matrix
> > > > > n = 1000 # number of output matrices
> > > > >
> > > > > # initializing the array ahead of time makes a big speed difference in R
> > > > > A = array(dim = c(l, m, n))
> > > > >
> > > > > # A function that returns a matrix of dimension l x m
> > > > > f = function(l, m){
> > > > >   tcrossprod(1:l, 1:m)
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > # For loops ---------------------------------------------------------------
> > > > >
> > > > > # My understanding is that R works fastest if it fills in the last dimension
> > > > > # of the array each time it goes through the for loop (the third dimension in
> > > > > # this case).  Other orderings would work, but I think they'd be slower.
> > > > > for(i in 1:n){
> > > > >   A[, , i] = f(l, m) * i
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > # Then you can pull out matrices like you'd expect using R's subset notation
> > > > >
> > > > > A[ , , 17] # the 17th l x m matrix
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > # a plyr way of doing things --------------------------------------------
> > > > > library(plyr)
> > > > > A2 = aaply(
> > > > >   1:n,
> > > > >   .margins = 1,
> > > > >   .fun = function(i){f(l, m) * i}
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > # Note that plyr arranges the data differently from my for loop:
> > > > > dim(A)
> > > > > dim(A2)
> > > > >
> > > > > # Otherwise, they return the same things:
> > > > > all(A[ , , 10] == A2[10, , ])
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > # Timing ------------------------------------------------------------------
> > > > >
> > > > > # we can compare how long the two methods take:
> > > > > system.time(
> > > > >   replicate(
> > > > >     100, {
> > > > >       A = array(dim = c(l, m, n))
> > > > >       for(i in 1:n){
> > > > >         A[, , i] = f(l, m) * i
> > > > >       }
> > > > >     }
> > > > >   )
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > system.time(
> > > > >   replicate(
> > > > >     100, {
> > > > >       aaply(
> > > > >         1:n,
> > > > >         .margins = 1,
> > > > >         .fun = function(i){f(l, m) * i}
> > > > >       )
> > > > >     }
> > > > >   )
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > # it looks like for-loops are *substantially* faster than plyr in this case.
> > > > > # This may be because I'm using plyr improperly or in a way it wasn't intended
> > > > >
> > > > > # For reference, let's see how much the whole array thing is slowing us down,
> > > > > # by just running the function for making matrices without the array overhead.
> > > > >
> > > > > system.time(
> > > > >   replicate(
> > > > >     100, {
> > > > >       for(i in 1:n){
> > > > >         sub.A = f(l, m) * i
> > > > >       }
> > > > >     }
> > > > >   )
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > # That took a few seconds less time on my machine than the arrays and for loops
> > > > > # So storing it in an array costs something like 3 seconds per thousand iterations

Searching Google for "convex polygon area R" turns up this function <http://rss.acs.unt.edu/Rdoc/library/aspace/html/calc_mcp.html>.  It calculates a convex hull and automatically determines the area.  Looks like it has some nice features for discarding outliers as well.

I don't know anything about map projections, but I think you'd want to make sure you had an equal-area projection for something like this, to make sure that the area was reasonable.

Robert has some spatial autocorrelation stuff in the dismo package, but I'm not sure if it's related to what you're interested in.

Hope this helps!

Dave

messages.body_plain:
I would recommend:

 - following the Google R style guide: http://google-styleguide.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/google-r-style.html (or at least sticking to a consistent style)
 - use version control software like git
 - unit test all of your core functions. Ideally, every function, but most scientists don't have that amount of time. Use packages like Hadley's testthat or Runit
 - separate your data from your code, i.e. all external data should come from read files, not hardcoded in the code (unless it's a constant).
 - write modular code
 - package large programs
 - follow idiomatic R, like avoiding for loops when a function from the *apply family would work
 - use data abstractions like classes, not just deeply nested lists
 - don't mix S3 and S4.
 - if a function is longer than a page, refactor (and break it up) so it's smaller
 - don't make up statistics or statistical techniques
 - document everything
 - use functional programming style where appropriate, i.e. closures, passing functions, etc
 - if you package or program is parallelized, always have an option for users that don't have more than one core.
 - be portable: i.e. don't use paste("path", "to", "file", sep="/") as this assumes "/' is your path separator. Use file.path() and similar portable functions.
 - if you write C extensions, they should compile with -Wall without warnings.

That's a pretty long list already! Some of these will obviously confuse beginners, but I figured it may be helpful for other folks here.

HTH,
Vince

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: 'Best Practices' for R-scripting
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: 'Best Practices' for R-scripting
messages.body_plain:
Marissa and Sebastian wrote this good set of tips for beginners for their course:

1. Any time you write a line of code more than once, program it as a function so you only have one place where you need to look for any corrections or changes.

2. Break your code down to individual functions that each preform an individual task so you can debug and test piece by piece (“functional decomposition”).

3. Plan out your code beforehand, writing a phrase or sentence for each general step you plan to take (these might be your functions), then breaking those into smaller steps, until each is something you can turn into a line of code (“pseudocoding”); this is analogous to outlining a paper before writing full sentences to make sure you have logical flow and all of the pieces fit together.

4. Comment while you code so it’s easier to remember what the code means when revisiting it.

5. Define parameters up front rather than using numbers within coded calculations so it’s easy to find and change them.

6. Write your code as a script instead of at the prompt so it’s easier to edit, save what worked, and run it again another day.

7. Specific to R (and Matlab): any time you can use vectors or matrices instead of for loops, try it; it’s usually much faster.

8. Debugging:

(a)  Test your functions for parameters/cases where you know the answer before running it for a more complicated case so you can make sure they work (“testing”).

(b)  When you can’t figure out a bug, go line-by-line through the function, checking that you’re getting what you expect from each command (“desk-checking”; R functions: debug, browser); you can also comment out lines to help you isolate a bug (in R, text after a #).

(c)  Especially for code where others might be using your functions, build in warning and error messages for inappropriate values that might accidently be passed (R functions: warning, stop; e.g., cases where zero or negative parameter values will give invalid results).

To all this I would add:

1) Check to see if someone else has done it first:  Search CRAN/Bioconductor packages, R-Bloggers, the R-help listserv, and Stack Overflow to see how others might have solved the problem.  No need to invent the wheel, and you'll learn from seeing how others approached your problem.

2) Commenting: Comment and organize your code as if you have to send the script to your advisor, or submit it with your publication.  Do this from the start.

messages.body_plain:
Hey Dave,

I just mean if you write classes (especially in a package), don't write some stuff in S3 and other stuff in S4. Both are fine for different tasks, but stick with one and use it per project. Mixing creates a nightmare in documentation, generics, and for users generally.

If you're doing analysis with two packages and one uses S3 and S4, this isn't want I mean by mixing — that's fine.

As an aside, folks using S4 should write getters and setters for object slots. Using @ directly is generally discouraged, as internal object consistency maybe screwed up. From top-level interactivity to bottom-level algorithms, the packages from Bioconductor's core team (like GenomicRanges) are great to learn from if you follow the "Use the source, Luke" learning strategy.

Vince

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I recently upgraded my version of Richard McElreath's rethinking package, and now some code that used to work is buggy.

I had previously used the handy "compare" function to generate a table of AICc values that I could then extract:

> compare(N,M0,nobs=length(d[,y])) #this will generate:

k AICc BIC w.AICc w.BIC dAICc dBIC
M0 4 5446.423 5464.356 1.00E+00 1.00E+00 0 0
N 3 5493.882 5507.341 4.95E-11 4.63E-10 47.45926 42.98531

> C=as.data.frame(compare(...as above...) #This allows me to access AICc values via
> C$AICc

With the new version of rethinking, the output table still shows up ok in the console, but the line of code to convert to a data frame kicks out an error: Error in as.data.frame.default(compare(N, M0, nobs = length(d[, y]))) :  cannot coerce class 'structure("compareIC", package = "rethinking")' into a data.frame

Debugging through the source code, it looks like everything works fine until the last line of the source code, which assigns the output data:

> new("compareIC", output = result)

And with that, I am out of my league. It looks like he (Richard) is now designating the output as some new data structure called a "compareIC", which I assume he just made up. I don't quite understand all the data structure components to R, but it looks like if I make up a function and designate the data as new("data.frame", ...), then I can access columns like I want to. I suppose I could write my own version of the "compare" function, but I'd rather not, as I use the old compare function in many pieces of code. So, my question is:
Is there a way to coerce this unknown structure into a data frame, or otherwise extract values from it? I can provide the entire "compare" source code if needed. Thought I'd try DRUG first, then on to the author himself (unless he happens to be on this list serve?)

Cheers,
Jens
